The subset fits. Keeping texts of 443 tokens or fewer retains all 450 reference solutions and 499 of the 561 arithmetic contexts, at 0.97 GB per layer, or 4.86 GB for five layers. That's within the 6 GB limit.

`compare7` scores positions from a list `CL` of (text, position, class) entries, so the existing labels can be reused once I map text indices into the subset. I'll save the subset and the index map and record the plan in the notes.

I'll also print `stats` to confirm whether a label marks the predicting position or the predicted token. Getting that off by one would make the depth analysis meaningless. No edits are active, so the pass will read the original model.

The convention is confirmed. A label `(i, x, class)` names target token `x` of text `i`, and both its logprob and its top-k come from position `x-1`. So the hidden states I need are also at `x-1`.

Number positions are scored as "the first digit among the top-k is the target digit". The lens for number classes will therefore pick the best digit token at each layer, which makes it directly comparable with how pass 7 graded the final layer.

This pass reads the original model, with no edits, on 949 texts. It returns hidden states after layers 17, 20, 22, 24 and 26, plus logprobs and top-5, so layer 26 can be calibrated against the tool's own top-1.

The pass returned all five layers for 949 texts. Now comes the depth diagnostic, which reads only projections of these real activations; no edit is involved.

At each number position I take the hidden state at `x-1` after layers 17, 20, 22, 24 and 26. I normalise it as the final norm does and score it against the 10 digit embedding rows.

Layer 26 is the check. Its best digit must match the first digit in the tool's own top-5 at nearly every position. If it doesn't, my lens has a bug and nothing else in the table can be trusted.

Then, for each class, I'll compare layers 22 and 24 with layer 26 in 2-by-2 tables:
- **Late overwrite:** many positions right at layer 22 or 24 but wrong at 26, out of proportion to the reverse flips, would point to late layers corrupting a formed answer. That would be a repairable mechanism.
- **Capacity:** if final errors are almost never right at an earlier layer, the error was formed, not lost.

Two results, one of them a correction.

**Calibration holds.** Layer 26 projected through the final norm gains picks the same first digit as the tool's own top-5 at 99.57% of 12,544 positions, so the lens is sound.

**Indexing correction.** `hidden_26` must be the output of the last layer (`model.layers.25`), so `hidden_l` is the output of layer l-1. That makes `hidden_17` the input of the full-attention layer 17. E13's construction therefore used layer-16 inputs where it needed layer-17 inputs. It's a one-layer approximation that I'll record; E13's measured effect is real either way.

**Depth result.** For operands, the choice is made in layers 17 to 19:
- First digits of problem numbers: 27% right before layer 17, 78% after layer 19, 79% at the end.
- First digits of earlier results: 34% before layer 17, 87% after layer 19.

After that, late flips are balanced (41 right-to-wrong against 41 wrong-to-right for first digits of problem numbers). Arithmetic results keep improving to the last layer, with 242 late fixes against 101 late losses overall. So there is no late overwrite to repair. The "33% right at an earlier layer" figure is chance at layer 17, not evidence.

The crisp remaining question is what the retrieval head reads when the operand comes out wrong. If its attention peak sits on the source of the wrongly chosen number, the head faithfully retrieved what the model asked for, and the error is in the plan upstream. If it sits on the correct source while the output is wrong, the failure is downstream in layers 18-19, which might be repairable. Pass 5 already holds layer 17 attention on two long multi-problem texts, so this may be answerable for free. I'll record the results and check what pass 5 stored.
